headline: Dry and warming all week, with Glendale and the other coastal valleys peaking in the upper 70s to mid 80s on Thanksgiving amid gusty offshore winds, before a cooler weekend and light rain on Sunday; at the beaches, a big swell and very high tides bring coastal flooding and high surf Wednesday and Thursday.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Monday night stays mild and dry around Glendale and across Los Angeles and Ventura counties, with clear skies and no marine layer at LAX this afternoon. It turns cold overnight in some spots, and very low clouds or fog are possible around Paso Robles overnight, but no rain is expected.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Offshore (Santa Ana–type) winds pick up Tuesday, with gusts around 30 mph from Santa Clarita and the nearby mountains through the Highway 126 corridor into the Oxnard plain and the northwest San Fernando Valley, staying below advisory levels. The tail end of a Pacific Northwest storm could bring very light rain to the Central Coast, mainly San Luis Obispo County, Tuesday night into Wednesday, though models have backed off on the chances; clouds cover most of the area Tuesday night into early Wednesday, then Wednesday turns sunny. The offshore winds drive a warming trend that peaks on Thanksgiving Thursday, when the coast and coastal valleys, including the Glendale area, reach the upper 70s to mid 80s while the higher valleys and interior stay cooler, and winds in those same wind-prone areas could strengthen enough for low-end wind advisories.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Friday stays warm and dry, and dry weather continues at least through Saturday, but temperatures cool over the weekend, especially at the coast and in the valleys, as winds turn onshore ahead of the next storm. That storm moves through mostly on Sunday, bringing at least some light rain to most areas: up to an inch on the Central Coast, especially its northern part, and likely under half an inch south of Point Conception, including Los Angeles County. At least one more storm is expected around next Tuesday, with 1–3 inches possible on mountain slopes facing the incoming storm.

coast: A large, long-period west swell arrives Tuesday and peaks Wednesday and Thursday, combining with very high tides to bring significant surf and significant coastal flooding; the worst is expected on the Central Coast and Ventura County beaches, with somewhat smaller but still concerning issues elsewhere, including many strong rip currents nearly everywhere, strong along-shore currents, a risk of sneaker waves, heavy shore break, beach erosion and possible breaking waves at harbor entrances. For the San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara Central Coast beaches, a Coastal Flood Advisory and High Surf Advisory run until 6 AM Wednesday, followed by a Coastal Flood Warning and High Surf Warning from 6 AM Wednesday to noon Thursday. Ventura County beaches have a Coastal Flood Advisory until 8 AM Wednesday and a High Surf Advisory from 9 PM Tuesday to 8 AM Wednesday, then a Coastal Flood Warning and High Surf Warning from 8 AM Wednesday to noon Thursday. The Malibu coast and Los Angeles County beaches have a Coastal Flood Advisory until 8 AM Wednesday, a Coastal Flood Watch from Wednesday morning through Thursday morning, and a High Surf Advisory from 6 AM Wednesday to 9 PM Thursday; the Santa Barbara south coast beaches and islands have a Coastal Flood Advisory until noon Thursday and a High Surf Advisory from 6 AM Wednesday to noon Thursday (to 9 PM Thursday for the islands). For boaters, winds and seas stay below small craft advisory levels through Tuesday. Small Craft Advisories run from 9 PM Tuesday (3 AM Wednesday for some waters) to 3 PM Thursday, with seas peaking at 14–18 feet on the outer waters Wednesday and Wednesday night and 13–16 feet north of Point Sal Wednesday. South of Point Conception, there is a 50–60 percent chance of advisory-level winds (and 30–40 percent for seas) in the western Santa Barbara Channel Wednesday and a 50–70 percent chance of advisory-level northeast winds (40–60 percent for seas) from Ventura to Santa Monica Thursday. Friday and Saturday bring lighter winds, though seas could stay at advisory levels on the outer waters (60–80 percent chance) and north of Point Sal (40–60 percent).
watch_for: Thanksgiving offshore winds possibly reaching low-end advisory levels around Santa Clarita, the Highway 126 corridor, the Oxnard plain and the northwest San Fernando Valley.
Coastal flood and high surf warnings Wednesday into Thursday, worst on the Central Coast and Ventura County beaches, with a Coastal Flood Watch for Los Angeles County beaches.
Rain totals with Sunday's storm and another possible storm around next Tuesday.
confidence: Forecasters are confident in the dry, warming stretch through Saturday, have lowered the already small chance of rain Tuesday night, and expect the Sunday and next-Tuesday storms with the usual uncertainty in rain amounts.
